card-cantor.title: Cantor's theorem
card-cantor.subject: functions
card-cantor.statement: For every set S there is no surjection S → P(S), while x ↦ {x} is an injection, so |S| < |P(S)|; consequently there is no set of all sets.

card-countable-closure.title: Products and countable unions of countable sets
card-countable-closure.subject: functions
card-countable-closure.statement: If A and B are countable then A × B is countable, so every finite product of countable sets is countable; and the union of countably many countable sets is countable.

card-countable.title: Countable sets
card-countable.subject: functions
card-countable.statement: S is countable if there is an injection S → ℕ, countably infinite if there is a bijection S → ℕ; finite sets are countable, and a non-empty countable set is the range of a sequence s₀, s₁, s₂, ….

card-csb.title: Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein theorem
card-csb.subject: functions
card-csb.statement: If there are injections f: A → B and g: B → A then there is a bijection A → B; that is, |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| together imply |A| = |B|.

card-equal.title: Equal cardinality
card-equal.subject: functions
card-equal.statement: For sets S and T, |S| = |T| means there exists a bijection S → T; equal cardinality is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and |S| < |T| means |S| ≤ |T| but not |S| = |T|.

card-leq.title: Comparing cardinalities
card-leq.subject: functions
card-leq.statement: For sets S and T, |S| ≤ |T| means there exists an injection S → T; this comparison is reflexive and transitive, and S ⊆ T implies |S| ≤ |T| via the inclusion map.

card-power-set.title: Power set
card-power-set.subject: functions
card-power-set.statement: The power set P(S) is the set of all subsets of S; U ↦ (indicator function of U) is a bijection from P(S) to the functions S → {0, 1}, so |P(S)| = 2ⁿ if S has n elements.

card-reals-uncountable.title: ℝ is uncountable
card-reals-uncountable.subject: functions
card-reals-uncountable.statement: ℝ is uncountable (|ℕ| < |ℝ|): for r₁, r₂, … in [0, 1] with fixed decimal expansions, s = 0.s₁s₂… with sᵢ = 2 if rᵢ has i-th digit 1, else 1, lies in [0, 1] but is no rᵢ.

card-z-q-countable.title: ℤ and ℚ are countably infinite
card-z-q-countable.subject: functions
card-z-q-countable.statement: |ℤ| = |ℚ| = |ℕ|: n ↦ (|n|, sgn(n) + 1) injects ℤ into ℕ × ℕ, and r ↦ (qr, q), with q the least positive integer such that qr ∈ ℤ, injects ℚ into ℤ × ℤ⁺.

cyc-def.title: Cyclic subgroups and cyclic groups
cyc-def.subject: group-theory
cyc-def.statement: For g ∈ G, ⟨g⟩ = {gᵏ : k ∈ ℤ} is the smallest subgroup of G containing g, and |⟨g⟩| = |g|; G is cyclic, with generator g, if G = ⟨g⟩, and every cyclic group is abelian.

cyc-subgroups.title: Subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic
cyc-subgroups.subject: group-theory
cyc-subgroups.statement: Every subgroup H ≠ {e} of G = ⟨g⟩ is ⟨gᵐ⟩ for the least m ∈ ℤ⁺ with gᵐ ∈ H, so subgroups of cyclic groups are cyclic; if |g| = n, ⟨gᵏ⟩ = ⟨gᵈ⟩ with d = gcd(k, n).

div-def.title: Divisibility
div-def.subject: number-theory
div-def.statement: For a, b ∈ ℤ, a ∣ b means there is k ∈ ℤ with b = ak; a is then a divisor of b.

div-properties.title: Basic properties of divisibility
div-properties.subject: number-theory
div-properties.statement: Divisibility is transitive, and if a ∣ b and a ∣ c then a ∣ (bx + cy) for all x, y ∈ ℤ.

eqv-classes.title: Equivalence classes and quotient set
eqv-classes.subject: relations
eqv-classes.statement: For an equivalence relation ∼ on a set A, the equivalence class of a ∈ A is [a] = {x ∈ A : x ∼ a}, and the quotient A/∼ is the set of all equivalence classes.

eqv-def.title: Equivalence relation
eqv-def.subject: relations
eqv-def.statement: A relation ∼ on a set A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

eqv-partition.title: Equivalence classes partition the set
eqv-partition.subject: relations
eqv-partition.statement: For an equivalence relation ∼ on A and a, b ∈ A: a ∈ [a]; [a] = [b] ⟺ a ∼ b; [a] ∩ [b] = ∅ ⟺ a ≁ b. Thus classes are non-empty, pairwise disjoint and cover A.

fn-bijective.title: Bijective function
fn-bijective.subject: functions
fn-bijective.statement: A function f: A → B is bijective (a bijection) if it is both injective and surjective, i.e. every t ∈ B equals f(s) for exactly one s ∈ A.

fn-binary-operator.title: Binary operator and identity element
fn-binary-operator.subject: functions
fn-binary-operator.statement: A binary operator on S is a function ∗: S × S → S; an identity element for ∗ is an e ∈ S with e ∗ a = a ∗ e = a for all a ∈ S.

fn-composition-preserves.title: Composites of injections, surjections and bijections
fn-composition-preserves.subject: functions
fn-composition-preserves.statement: For f: A → B and g: B → C: if f and g are injective so is g ∘ f, if f and g are surjective so is g ∘ f, so a composite of bijections is a bijection.

fn-composition.title: Function composition and identity functions
fn-composition.subject: functions
fn-composition.statement: For f: A → B and g: B → C, (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) defines g ∘ f: A → C; composition is associative, and id_A(x) = x satisfies f ∘ id_A = f = id_B ∘ f.

fn-def.title: Function
fn-def.subject: functions
fn-def.statement: A function f: A → B is a left-total, functional relation between A and B, so each a ∈ A is related to exactly one element f(a) ∈ B; its graph is Γ(f) = {(a, f(a)) : a ∈ A}.

fn-equality.title: Equality of functions
fn-equality.subject: functions
fn-equality.statement: Functions f: A → B and g: C → D are equal if and only if A = C, B = D and f(a) = g(a) for every a ∈ A, so changing only the codomain gives a different function.

fn-image.title: Image of a set and range
fn-image.subject: functions
fn-image.statement: For a function f: A → B and U ⊆ A, the image of U is f(U) = {f(x) : x ∈ U} ⊆ B, and the range of f is f(A), which need not equal the codomain B.

fn-injective.title: Injective function
fn-injective.subject: functions
fn-injective.statement: A function f: A → B is injective (one-to-one) if f(s₁) = f(s₂) implies s₁ = s₂ for all s₁, s₂ ∈ A; it fails to be injective exactly when some s₁ ≠ s₂ in A have f(s₁) = f(s₂).

fn-inverse-function.title: Inverse function
fn-inverse-function.subject: functions
fn-inverse-function.statement: f: A → B is invertible if some g: B → A has g ∘ f = id_A and f ∘ g = id_B; such g is unique, written f⁻¹, and for A = B is f's inverse under composition.

fn-invertible-iff-bijective.title: Invertible iff bijective
fn-invertible-iff-bijective.subject: functions
fn-invertible-iff-bijective.statement: A function f: A → B is invertible if and only if it is bijective, in which case f⁻¹(t) is the unique s ∈ A with f(s) = t and f⁻¹: B → A is itself a bijection.

fn-operator-inverse.title: Inverse with respect to an operator
fn-operator-inverse.subject: functions
fn-operator-inverse.statement: For a binary operator ∗ on S with identity e, an inverse of a ∈ S is b ∈ S with a ∗ b = b ∗ a = e, written a⁻¹; 0 has none under × on ℝ.

fn-preimage.title: Preimage of a set
fn-preimage.subject: functions
fn-preimage.statement: For a function f: A → B and V ⊆ B, the preimage of V is f⁻¹(V) = {x ∈ A : f(x) ∈ V} ⊆ A, defined for every function whether or not f has an inverse.

fn-surjective.title: Surjective function
fn-surjective.subject: functions
fn-surjective.statement: A function f: A → B is surjective (onto) if every t ∈ B is f(s) for some s ∈ A, i.e. f(A) = B; otherwise some t ∈ B is f(s) for no s ∈ A.

gcd-bezout-cor.title: Consequences of Bézout
gcd-bezout-cor.subject: number-theory
gcd-bezout-cor.statement: If d ∣ a and d ∣ b then d ∣ gcd(a, b); a and b are coprime iff au + bv = 1 for some u, v; and if gcd(a, b) = 1 with a ∣ bc then a ∣ c.

gcd-bezout.title: Bézout's Identity
gcd-bezout.subject: number-theory
gcd-bezout.statement: For a, b not both zero there exist u, v ∈ ℤ with au + bv = gcd(a, b); indeed gcd(a, b) is the least positive integer of that form.

gcd-def.title: Greatest common divisor and coprimality
gcd-def.subject: number-theory
gcd-def.statement: gcd(a, b) is the largest integer dividing both a and b (not both zero); a and b are coprime when gcd(a, b) = 1.

gcd-division-algorithm.title: Division Algorithm
gcd-division-algorithm.subject: number-theory
gcd-division-algorithm.statement: For a ∈ ℤ and b ∈ ℤ⁺ there exist unique q, r ∈ ℤ with a = qb + r and 0 ≤ r < b.

gcd-euclidean.title: Euclidean Algorithm
gcd-euclidean.subject: number-theory
gcd-euclidean.statement: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); iterating the division algorithm terminates at the last non-zero remainder, which is gcd(a, b).

gcd-wop.title: Well-Ordering Principle
gcd-wop.subject: number-theory
gcd-wop.statement: Every non-empty set of non-negative integers has a least element.

grp-abelian.title: Abelian groups
grp-abelian.subject: group-theory
grp-abelian.statement: A group G is abelian (commutative) if ab = ba for all a, b ∈ G; equivalently, (ab)⁻¹ = a⁻¹b⁻¹ for all a, b ∈ G.

grp-def.title: Group
grp-def.subject: group-theory
grp-def.statement: A group (G, ·) is a set G with an associative binary operator · having an identity e (e·a = a·e = a) and giving each a ∈ G an inverse a⁻¹ ∈ G with a·a⁻¹ = a⁻¹·a = e.

grp-dihedral.title: The dihedral group Dₙ
grp-dihedral.subject: group-theory
grp-dihedral.statement: The symmetries of a regular n-gon (n ≥ 3) form a non-abelian group Dₙ of 2n elements rⁱ, srⁱ (0 ≤ i < n), for r the 2π/n rotation, s a reflection; rⁿ = s² = e, sr = r⁻¹s.

grp-properties.title: Basic properties of groups
grp-properties.subject: group-theory
grp-properties.statement: In a group the identity and each inverse are unique; ab = ac or ba = ca implies b = c; (a⁻¹)⁻¹ = a; and (a₁⋯aₖ)⁻¹ = aₖ⁻¹⋯a₁⁻¹, so (ab)⁻¹ = b⁻¹a⁻¹ and (aⁿ)⁻¹ = (a⁻¹)ⁿ = a⁻ⁿ.

grp-symmetric.title: The symmetric group Sₙ
grp-symmetric.subject: group-theory
grp-symmetric.statement: For a set X, the bijections X → X form a group S_X under composition, with identity id_X and inverses the inverse functions; Sₙ = S_X for X = {1, …, n} is abelian iff n ≤ 2.

grp-zn.title: The groups ℤₙ and ℤₙ*
grp-zn.subject: group-theory
grp-zn.statement: (ℤₙ, +) is an abelian group of order n with identity [0] and −[a] = [n−a]; under multiplication, ℤₙ* = {[a] : gcd(a, n) = 1} is an abelian group and ℤₙ is not a group if n ≥ 2.

hom-def.title: Group homomorphism
hom-def.subject: group-theory
hom-def.statement: For groups (G, ·) and (H, ⋆), a function φ: G → H is a homomorphism if φ(x·y) = φ(x) ⋆ φ(y) for all x, y ∈ G.

hom-kernel.title: Kernel and image
hom-kernel.subject: group-theory
hom-kernel.statement: For a homomorphism φ: G → H, ker φ = {g ∈ G : φ(g) = e_H} is a subgroup of G, im φ = φ(G) is a subgroup of H, and φ is injective iff ker φ = {e_G}.

hom-properties.title: Properties of homomorphisms
hom-properties.subject: group-theory
hom-properties.statement: For a homomorphism φ: G → H, φ(e_G) = e_H, φ(gⁿ) = φ(g)ⁿ (n ∈ ℤ), |φ(g)| divides |g| if finite, φ(K) ≤ H for K ≤ G, cyclic (abelian) if K is; φ⁻¹(L) ≤ G for L ≤ H.

impl-contrapositive-proof.title: Proof by contrapositive
impl-contrapositive-proof.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-contrapositive-proof.statement: To prove P ⟹ Q it suffices to prove ¬Q ⟹ ¬P; e.g. for n ∈ ℤ, n² even ⟹ n even, because odd n = 2k + 1 gives n² = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd.

impl-contrapositive.title: Contrapositive of an implication
impl-contrapositive.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-contrapositive.statement: For propositions P and Q, the contrapositive ¬Q ⟹ ¬P of P ⟹ Q is logically equivalent to it: the two have the same truth value in every case.

impl-converse.title: Converse of an implication
impl-converse.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-converse.statement: The converse of P ⟹ Q is Q ⟹ P; it is not logically equivalent to P ⟹ Q, so a true implication can have a false converse.

impl-def.title: Implication
impl-def.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-def.statement: For propositions P and Q, the implication P ⟹ Q ('if P then Q', with hypothesis P and conclusion Q) is false when P is true and Q is false, and true in the other three cases.

impl-iff.title: If and only if
impl-iff.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-iff.statement: P ⟺ Q ('P if and only if Q') means (P ⟹ Q) ∧ (Q ⟹ P); it is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value, so proving it requires proving both directions.

impl-nec-suff.title: Necessary and sufficient conditions
impl-nec-suff.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-nec-suff.statement: 'P is sufficient for Q' means P ⟹ Q, 'P is necessary for Q' means Q ⟹ P, and 'P is necessary and sufficient for Q' means P ⟺ Q.

impl-negation.title: Negating an implication
impl-negation.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-negation.statement: ¬(P ⟹ Q) is logically equivalent to P ∧ ¬Q, so ¬(∀x ∈ S, P(x) ⟹ Q(x)) is equivalent to ∃x ∈ S, P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x): a universal implication is refuted by one counterexample.

impl-vacuous.title: Vacuous truth
impl-vacuous.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
impl-vacuous.statement: If P is false then P ⟹ Q is true whatever Q is; in particular ∀x ∈ ∅, P(x) is true for every predicate P, since no element can fail P.

ind-principle.title: Principle of Mathematical Induction
ind-principle.subject: induction
ind-principle.statement: If P(n) is a predicate on ℤ⁺ such that P(1) is true and P(k) ⟹ P(k + 1) for every k ∈ ℤ⁺, then P(n) is true for every n ∈ ℤ⁺.

ind-proof-format.title: Writing a proof by induction
ind-proof-format.subject: induction
ind-proof-format.statement: To prove P(n) for all n ∈ ℤ⁺, verify P(1), assume P(k) for arbitrary k and derive P(k + 1); e.g. 5 ∣ 6ⁿ − 1, since 6ᵏ − 1 = 5d gives 6ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 5(6ᵏ + d).

iso-cyclic.title: Classification of cyclic groups
iso-cyclic.subject: group-theory
iso-cyclic.statement: If G = ⟨g⟩ is infinite, k ↦ gᵏ is an isomorphism ℤ → G; if |G| = n, [k]ₙ ↦ gᵏ is one ℤₙ → G. So every cyclic group is isomorphic to ℤ or to exactly one ℤₙ.

iso-def.title: Isomorphism
iso-def.subject: group-theory
iso-def.statement: An isomorphism is a bijective homomorphism; G ≅ H if one G → H exists. Identities, inverses and composites of isomorphisms are isomorphisms, so ≅ is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and automorphisms of G form a group Aut(G) under composition.

iso-invariants.title: Isomorphism invariants
iso-invariants.subject: group-theory
iso-invariants.statement: If φ: G → H is an isomorphism, |G| = |H|, |φ(g)| = |g|, K ≅ φ(K) ≤ H for K ≤ G, and G is abelian (cyclic) iff H is; groups differing in any of these are not isomorphic.

lde-def.title: Linear Diophantine equations
lde-def.subject: number-theory
lde-def.statement: A linear Diophantine equation is ax + by = c with a, b, c ∈ ℤ, to be solved for integers x and y.

lde-general.title: General solution
lde-general.subject: number-theory
lde-general.statement: For a, b nonzero with d = gcd(a, b): if (x₀, y₀) solves ax + by = c, every solution is x = x₀ + (b/d)t, y = y₀ − (a/d)t for t ∈ ℤ.

lde-nonneg.title: Non-negative solutions
lde-nonneg.subject: number-theory
lde-nonneg.statement: Requiring x, y ≥ 0 restricts the parameter t to an interval, so a solvable equation may still have no, finitely many, or infinitely many non-negative solutions.

lde-solvable.title: Solvability criterion
lde-solvable.subject: number-theory
lde-solvable.statement: ax + by = c has an integer solution if and only if gcd(a, b) divides c.

mod-arithmetic.title: Arithmetic of congruences
mod-arithmetic.subject: number-theory
mod-arithmetic.statement: State and prove that congruence is compatible with + and ×, so a ≡ r, b ≡ s (mod n) ⟹ a+b ≡ r+s and ab ≡ rs (mod n).

mod-congruence-def.title: Congruence modulo n
mod-congruence-def.subject: number-theory
mod-congruence-def.statement: a ≡ b (mod n) means n ∣ (b − a); equivalently, a and b leave the same remainder on division by n.

mod-equivalence.title: Congruence is an equivalence relation
mod-equivalence.subject: number-theory
mod-equivalence.statement: For fixed n, ≡ (mod n) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it partitions ℤ into n congruence classes.

mod-inverses.title: Multiplicative inverses in ℤₙ
mod-inverses.subject: number-theory
mod-inverses.statement: [a] is invertible in ℤₙ iff gcd(a,n)=1; the inverse is computed from a Bézout identity au+nv=1.

mod-lastdigit.title: Last-digit computation
mod-lastdigit.subject: number-theory
mod-lastdigit.statement: The last digit of an integer m is m mod 10; combined with compatibility, aᵏ mod 10 is found by reducing at each step.

mod-zn.title: The integers modulo n (ℤₙ)
mod-zn.subject: number-theory
mod-zn.statement: ℤₙ = {[0],…,[n−1]} with well-defined +, × inherited from ℤ; it is a commutative ring with identity.

ord-def.title: Partial and total orders (posets)
ord-def.subject: relations
ord-def.statement: ⪯ on A is a (weak) partial order if reflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive, a strong order if irreflexive, anti-symmetric and transitive, and total (linear) if any two distinct elements are comparable; a set with a partial order is a poset.

ord-max.title: Maximal elements and the maximum
ord-max.subject: relations
ord-max.statement: In a poset, a is maximal if a ⪯ x ⟹ x = a, minimal if x ⪯ a ⟹ x = a, the maximum if x ⪯ a ∀x (dually, minimum); a maximum is unique and maximal, not conversely.

ord-sup-inf.title: Bounds, supremum and infimum
ord-sup-inf.subject: relations
ord-sup-inf.statement: In a poset (A, ⪯), U is an upper bound of S ⊆ A if x ⪯ U ∀x ∈ S; a supremum is an upper bound ⪯ all others, and is unique; lower bounds and infima are dual.

pf-contradiction.title: Proof by contradiction
pf-contradiction.subject: relations
pf-contradiction.statement: To prove a statement T, assume ¬T and derive a contradiction R ∧ ¬R; this is valid because ¬T ⟹ (R ∧ ¬R) is logically equivalent to T, and it may prove that something exists without identifying it.

pf-sqrt2.title: √2 is irrational
pf-sqrt2.subject: relations
pf-sqrt2.statement: √2 is irrational: there are no integers p, q with q ≠ 0 and p² = 2q².

prime-def.title: Prime and composite integers
prime-def.subject: number-theory
prime-def.statement: An integer p > 1 is prime when its only positive divisors are 1 and p; an integer n > 1 that is not prime is composite.

prime-euclid-lemma.title: Euclid's Lemma
prime-euclid-lemma.subject: number-theory
prime-euclid-lemma.statement: If p is prime and p ∣ ab, then p ∣ a or p ∣ b.

prime-fta.title: Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
prime-fta.subject: number-theory
prime-fta.statement: Every integer n > 1 is a product of primes, and that factorisation is unique up to the order of the factors.

prop-connectives.title: Conjunction, disjunction and negation
prop-connectives.subject: sets-and-propositions
prop-connectives.statement: For propositions P and Q, the conjunction P ∧ Q is true exactly when both are true, the disjunction P ∨ Q exactly when at least one is true (inclusive or), and the negation ¬P exactly when P is false.

prop-de-morgan.title: De Morgan's laws
prop-de-morgan.subject: sets-and-propositions
prop-de-morgan.statement: For all propositions P and Q, ¬(P ∧ Q) is logically equivalent to ¬P ∨ ¬Q, and ¬(P ∨ Q) is logically equivalent to ¬P ∧ ¬Q.

prop-predicate.title: Predicates
prop-predicate.subject: sets-and-propositions
prop-predicate.statement: A predicate P(x) is a statement containing a variable x whose truth value depends on x; substituting a value for x yields a proposition, so x² > π is a predicate and 2² > π a true proposition.

prop-proposition.title: Propositions
prop-proposition.subject: sets-and-propositions
prop-proposition.statement: A proposition is a statement with a definite truth value: it is either true or false, never both and never neither, whether or not that value is currently known.

prop-truth-tables.title: Truth tables and logical equivalence
prop-truth-tables.subject: sets-and-propositions
prop-truth-tables.statement: A truth table lists the truth value of a compound proposition under each of the 2ⁿ assignments of T/F to its n component propositions; two compound propositions are logically equivalent when their truth tables agree in every row.

quant-exists.title: Existential quantifier
quant-exists.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
quant-exists.statement: For a set S and predicate P(x), the proposition ∃x ∈ S, P(x) ('there exists x in S such that P(x)') is true exactly when P(x) is true for at least one x ∈ S.

quant-forall.title: Universal quantifier
quant-forall.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
quant-forall.statement: For a set S and predicate P(x), the proposition ∀x ∈ S, P(x) ('for all x in S') is true exactly when P(x) is true for every x ∈ S; one x ∈ S with P(x) false makes it false.

quant-negation.title: Negating quantifiers
quant-negation.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
quant-negation.statement: For a set S and predicate P(x), ¬(∀x ∈ S, P(x)) is equivalent to ∃x ∈ S, ¬P(x), and ¬(∃x ∈ S, P(x)) to ∀x ∈ S, ¬P(x); nested quantifiers are negated one by one, left to right, keeping domains.

quant-order.title: Order of quantifiers
quant-order.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
quant-order.statement: Adjacent quantifiers of the same kind commute, but ∃y ∀x P(x, y) implies ∀x ∃y P(x, y), not conversely: over ℝ, ∀x ∃y, x + y = 0 is true while ∃y ∀x, x + y = 0 is false.

quant-proof-methods.title: Proving quantified statements
quant-proof-methods.subject: quantifiers-and-implications
quant-proof-methods.statement: To prove ∀x ∈ S, P(x), fix an arbitrary x ∈ S and prove P(x) using only that x ∈ S; to prove ∃x ∈ S, P(x), exhibit one specific witness x₀ ∈ S and verify P(x₀).

read-definition.title: Mathematical definition
read-definition.subject: reading-mathematics
read-definition.statement: A mathematical definition is a complete, precise criterion: an object has the defined property exactly when it satisfies the condition, so every case, edge cases included, is settled by that condition (or a logically equivalent one), not by intuition.

read-direct-proof.title: Anatomy of a direct proof
read-direct-proof.subject: reading-mathematics
read-direct-proof.statement: A direct proof of 'if H then C' assumes H for arbitrary objects, unpacks definitions, computes until C's defining form appears, states C and ends with □, explaining each step in words; e.g. ab = (2m₁)(2m₂) = 2(2m₁m₂) is even.

read-even-odd.title: Even and odd integers
read-even-odd.subject: reading-mathematics
read-even-odd.statement: An integer n is even if n = 2m for some m ∈ ℤ, and odd if n = 2m + 1 for some m ∈ ℤ; e.g. 0 = 2·0 is even, −7 = 2·(−4) + 1 is odd.

read-examples-nonexamples.title: Examples and non-examples
read-examples-nonexamples.subject: reading-mathematics
read-examples-nonexamples.statement: After reading a new definition, test it on a deliberately varied sample: several objects satisfying it, at least one that does not, and edge cases such as 0, negatives and extremes, deciding each strictly by the condition and stating why.

read-hypothesis-conclusion.title: Hypothesis and conclusion
read-hypothesis-conclusion.subject: reading-mathematics
read-hypothesis-conclusion.statement: Every mathematical result has a hypothesis (the conditions assumed) and a conclusion (guaranteed whenever they hold), e.g. 'if a and b are even integers, then ab is even'; it asserts nothing where its hypothesis fails, and may leave it implicit.

read-kinds-of-results.title: Lemma, proposition, theorem, corollary
read-kinds-of-results.subject: reading-mathematics
read-kinds-of-results.statement: Mathematical results are precise claims about defined objects, labelled by role: lemma, a stepping stone to a larger result; proposition, a useful result of moderate importance; theorem, a major or central result; corollary, an almost immediate consequence of a theorem.

read-proof-generality.title: Generality in proofs
read-proof-generality.subject: reading-mathematics
read-proof-generality.statement: Reasoning about arbitrary objects, using only what the hypothesis grants, proves a result for all objects satisfying it; checking particular values does not. Unneeded hypotheses can be dropped: if a is even, ab is even for every integer b.

read-proof.title: Proof
read-proof.subject: reading-mathematics
read-proof.statement: A proof is a finite chain of statements from hypothesis to conclusion, each justified by the hypothesis, a definition, an axiom, a previously proven result, or logical deduction from earlier lines; it makes the result certain wherever the hypothesis holds.

read-proving-vs-applying.title: Proving vs applying a theorem
read-proving-vs-applying.subject: reading-mathematics
read-proving-vs-applying.statement: To prove a result, assume its hypothesis and derive its conclusion, without asking whether the hypothesis holds for anything; to apply it, first verify its hypothesis for the particular objects at hand, and only then assert the conclusion for them.

read-self-explanation.title: Self-explanation
read-self-explanation.subject: reading-mathematics
read-self-explanation.statement: To self-explain a proof, after each line identify its main idea, how it follows from earlier lines, definitions or known results, and what question it raises; paraphrasing (restating) or monitoring (noting understanding) adds no logical connection and is not self-explanation.

rec-fibonacci.title: The Fibonacci sequence
rec-fibonacci.subject: induction
rec-fibonacci.statement: The Fibonacci sequence, x₁ = x₂ = 1 and xₙ = xₙ₋₁ + xₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 3, satisfies xₙ = (αⁿ − βⁿ)/√5 for every n ∈ ℤ⁺, where α = (1 + √5)/2, β = (1 − √5)/2.

rec-recursive-def.title: Recursive definitions
rec-recursive-def.subject: induction
rec-recursive-def.statement: A recursive definition of a set S gives basis elements and constructors; S consists exactly of the elements obtained from the basis by finitely many constructor applications. A recursive sequence fixes initial terms and defines later terms from earlier ones.

rec-structural-induction.title: Principle of Structural Induction
rec-structural-induction.subject: induction
rec-structural-induction.statement: Let S be recursively defined; if P(b) holds for every basis element b and, for each constructor, P holds for the output whenever it holds for all inputs, then P(s) holds for every s ∈ S.

rel-checking.title: Verifying and refuting relation properties
rel-checking.subject: relations
rel-checking.statement: Each relation property is universally quantified, so it is verified by a proof for arbitrary elements and refuted by one counterexample; e.g. a ∼ b ⟺ ab > 1 on ℝ⁺ is symmetric but not reflexive, total, or transitive.

rel-def.title: Binary relation
rel-def.subject: relations
rel-def.statement: A binary relation R between sets A and B is a subset of A × B, with aRb meaning (a, b) ∈ R; A is its domain, B its codomain; if B = A, R is a relation on A.

rel-left-total-functional.title: Left-total and functional relations
rel-left-total-functional.subject: relations
rel-left-total-functional.statement: R ⊆ A×B is left-total if each a ∈ A has some b ∈ B with aRb, and functional if aRb ∧ aRc ⟹ b=c (∀a ∈ A, b,c ∈ B): at least one, respectively at most one, partner.

rel-properties.title: Properties of relations on a set
rel-properties.subject: relations
rel-properties.statement: R on A is reflexive if aRa, irreflexive if ¬aRa, symmetric if aRb ⟹ bRa, anti-symmetric if aRb ∧ bRa ⟹ a=b, transitive if aRb ∧ bRc ⟹ aRc, total if a=b ∨ aRb ∨ bRa (∀a,b,c ∈ A).

set-builder.title: Set-builder notation
set-builder.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-builder.statement: For a set U and predicate P(x), {x ∈ U : P(x)} is the set of x ∈ U with P(x) true; generally, {expression : conditions} is the set of values the expression takes as its variables satisfy the conditions.

set-cartesian-product.title: Cartesian product
set-cartesian-product.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-cartesian-product.statement: For sets A and B, the Cartesian product A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A, b ∈ B} consists of ordered pairs, where (a, b) = (c, d) exactly when a = c and b = d.

set-def.title: Sets, elements and the empty set
set-def.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-def.statement: A set is an unordered collection of well-defined, distinct objects, its elements (x ∈ S: x is an element of S); two sets are equal exactly when they have the same elements, and the empty set ∅ has none.

set-difference-complement.title: Set difference and complement
set-difference-complement.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-difference-complement.statement: For sets S and T, the difference is S ∖ T = {x ∈ S : x ∉ T}; for a universe of discourse U and A ⊆ U, the complement of A is Aᶜ = U ∖ A.

set-double-inclusion.title: Set equality by double inclusion
set-double-inclusion.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-double-inclusion.statement: For sets S and T, S = T if and only if S ⊆ T and T ⊆ S, so an equality of sets is proved by establishing the two inclusions separately.

set-number-sets.title: Standard number sets
set-number-sets.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-number-sets.statement: ℤ⁺ = {1, 2, 3, …} ⊆ ℤ* = {0, 1, 2, …} ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ = {a/b : a, b ∈ ℤ, b ≠ 0} ⊆ ℝ are the positive integers, non-negative integers, integers, rationals and reals.

set-subset.title: Subsets
set-subset.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-subset.statement: For sets S and T, S is a subset of T (S ⊆ T) when every element of S is in T, proved by showing each x ∈ S lies in T; thus S ⊆ S and ∅ ⊆ S.

set-union-intersection.title: Union and intersection
set-union-intersection.subject: sets-and-propositions
set-union-intersection.statement: For sets S and T, the union S ∪ T = {x : x ∈ S or x ∈ T}, with inclusive or, and the intersection S ∩ T = {x : x ∈ S and x ∈ T}.

sind-generalized.title: Induction from any base and step
sind-generalized.subject: induction
sind-generalized.statement: For a ∈ ℤ, d ∈ ℤ⁺: if P(a) holds and P(k) ⟹ P(k + d) for all k ∈ A = {a, a + d, …}, then P holds on A; d = 1 gives induction from base a.

sind-postage.title: Postage with 3¢ and 5¢ stamps
sind-postage.subject: induction
sind-postage.statement: Every integer n ≥ 8 is 3a + 5b with a, b ∈ ℤ*: 8 = 3 + 5, 9 = 3·3, 10 = 2·5, and k + 1 = (k − 2) + 3 for k ≥ 10.

sind-principle.title: Principle of Strong Induction
sind-principle.subject: induction
sind-principle.statement: For integers n₀ ≤ n₁: if P(n₀), …, P(n₁) hold and P(n₀) ∧ ⋯ ∧ P(k) ⟹ P(k + 1) for all k ≥ n₁, then P(n) holds for all n ≥ n₀; it is equivalent to ordinary induction.

sub-def.title: Subgroup
sub-def.subject: group-theory
sub-def.statement: A subset H of a group G is a subgroup, written H ≤ G, if H is a group under the operation of G; equivalently, e ∈ H and H is closed under products and inverses.

sub-order-divides.title: Order divides exponent
sub-order-divides.subject: group-theory
sub-order-divides.statement: If |g| = n is finite, gᵏ = e iff n ∣ k, and gⁱ = gʲ iff i ≡ j (mod n), so e, g, …, gⁿ⁻¹ are distinct; if |g| = ∞, distinct exponents give distinct powers.

sub-order-power.title: Order of a power
sub-order-power.subject: group-theory
sub-order-power.statement: If g ∈ G has finite order n and k ∈ ℤ, then |gᵏ| = n / gcd(n, k); in particular |gᵏ| divides n, and gᵏ has order n if and only if gcd(n, k) = 1.

sub-order.title: Order of a group and of an element
sub-order.subject: group-theory
sub-order.statement: The order |G| of a group is its number of elements; the order |g| of g ∈ G is the least n ∈ ℤ⁺ with gⁿ = e, or |g| = ∞ if no positive power of g equals e.

sub-test.title: Subgroup test
sub-test.subject: group-theory
sub-test.statement: A nonempty subset H of a group G is a subgroup if and only if ab⁻¹ ∈ H for all a, b ∈ H, and also if and only if H is closed under products and inverses.

sum-induction.title: Proving summation identities by induction
sum-induction.subject: induction
sum-induction.statement: To prove ∑ₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖ = F(n) for all n ∈ ℤ⁺, check a₁ = F(1) and, peeling off the last term, show F(k) + aₖ₊₁ = F(k + 1); for example ∑ₖ₌₁ⁿ 1/(k(k + 1)) = n/(n + 1).

sum-sigma.title: Sigma notation
sum-sigma.subject: induction
sum-sigma.statement: For integers n ≤ m, ∑ᵢ₌ₙᵐ rᵢ = rₙ + rₙ₊₁ + ⋯ + rₘ, with dummy index i, bounds n and m, and summand rᵢ; recursively, ∑ᵢ₌ₙⁿ rᵢ = rₙ and ∑ᵢ₌ₙᵐ⁺¹ rᵢ = ∑ᵢ₌ₙᵐ rᵢ + rₘ₊₁.
